clinicalPearls: Congenital anomaly caused by oblique insertion of the optic nerve into the globe, producing an ovoid disc with a raised superotemporal and depressed inferonasal margin.
Almost always bilateral though frequently asymmetric; the disc long axis is typically directed inferonasally.
Situs inversus of the retinal vessels is a characteristic sign, with vessels emerging in an anomalous nasal direction before doubling back.
An inferonasal fundus ectasia (staphylomatous crescent) and thinning of the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid accompany the tilt.
Refractive error is usually myopic astigmatism with the astigmatic axis oriented obliquely along the ectasia.
Superotemporal visual field defects that characteristically do NOT respect the vertical midline help distinguish it from chiasmal compression.
Refracting the patient and repeating perimetry after correcting the induced myopic defocus can abolish the pseudo-bitemporal field loss.
Considered a mild form of the optic disc dysplasia/coloboma spectrum and is usually a benign, non-progressive finding.
reference.pathophysiology: Tilted disc syndrome arises from incomplete or abnormal closure of the embryonic fetal fissure and an oblique entry of the optic nerve through the scleral canal during development. The result is an obliquely inserted, ovoid optic disc with the superotemporal portion elevated and the inferonasal portion recessed, accompanied by an inferonasal ectasia in which the retinal pigment epithelium, choroid and sclera are attenuated. This localised ectasia distorts the regional refractive geometry, producing myopic astigmatism, and the associated retinal thinning creates relative field depression corresponding to the ectatic zone. Because the anomaly straddles but does not strictly honour the vertical raphe, field defects mimic but do not truly respect the vertical meridian.
additionalDifferentials: Chiasmal compression from pituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma
additionalInvestigations: Automated static perimetry with refractive correction in place
Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve head and peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer
Cycloplegic refraction to characterise myopic astigmatism
Fundus photography documenting situs inversus and inferonasal crescent
Fundus autofluorescence to delineate peripapillary RPE changes
Neuroimaging (MRI of the sella/chiasm) when field defect respects the vertical midline or is progressive
redFlags: Visual field defect that strictly respects the vertical midline, suggesting a chiasmal lesion rather than the disc anomaly
Progressive field loss or new dyschromatopsia on follow-up
Development of a serous macular detachment or subretinal fluid
Choroidal neovascular membrane presenting with sudden central distortion
reference.prognosis: Vision is generally stable and good once refractive error is corrected, and the anomaly itself is non-progressive. Rarely, associated maculopathy such as serous detachment or choroidal neovascularisation may threaten central acuity.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the pseudo-bitemporal field defect as chiasmal compression and initiating unnecessary neuroimaging without first correcting refraction and repeating perimetry.
Overlooking associated inferonasal serous retinal detachment or choroidal neovascularisation as the cause of new symptoms.
Attributing the ovoid disc appearance to glaucoma and treating for raised intraocular pressure inappropriately.
Failing to recognise associated systemic or midline associations in syndromic cases.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
